entries.title: Tens of thousands continue to protest across France
entries.summary: Some 106,000 people marched through French cities for a fifth consecutive weekend of protests, marking the lowest turnout in recent weeks.
entries.content:
France

Tens of thousands continue to protest across France

November 15, 2026

Some 106,000 people marched through French cities for a fifth consecutive weekend of protests, marking the lowest turnout in recent weeks.

Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday to demonstrate against the rising cost of living and strained public services, the Interior Ministry said.

Saturday's demonstrations drew their lowest turnout in recent weeks. Some 106,000 people marched through French cities, with 24,000 in Paris alone. The previous weekend, some 146,000 people had participated nationwide.

The number of arrests was also significantly lower. Police detained 219 people across the country, according to the Interior Ministry.

Although the demonstrations were largely peaceful, police fired tear gas in Paris, Bordeaux and the western city of Nantes, including after some protesters shot fireworks.

France's protests expose deeper anger

Mass protests have swept across the European Union's second-largest economy for more than a month.

What began in September as student protests against teacher shortages and poor facilities has since evolved into a broader movement fuelled by anger over the rising cost of living, strained public services and police brutality.

In mid-October, around 565,000 people took to the streets across France, as riots, looting and clashes disrupted demonstrations in several cities.

As France entered its fifth consecutive weekend of nationwide unrest, President Emmanuel Macron's approval ratings fell to the lowest level since he took office in 2017, according to recent polls.

The French government doesn't have much room to respond to the protesters' demands due to its high debt.

entries.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
entries.summary: Eleven countries took part in the competition in Bangkok. Teenage winner Carmelle Collado's winning dance song is a tribute to Filipino women.
entries.content:
November 14, 2026

Eleven countries took part in the competition in Bangkok. Teenage winner Carmelle Collado's winning dance song is a tribute to Filipino women.

The Phillippines on Saturday became the first winner of the Asian version of the Eurovision Song Contest. 

Who took part in the event and which songs were featured?

Eleven countries, including South Korea, Malaysia and Vietnam, took part in the song contest in the Thai capital, Bangkok. However, major nations in the region such as China, Japan and India were absent from the event. 

19-year-old Carmelle Collado's dance song "Sobra-Sobra" (Too Much) won the competition. The song, which features lyrics in both English and Tagalog, is an empowering tribute to Filipino women.

The Philippines received 211 points in the competition, with Thailand in second place with 170 points. Vietnam placed third with 164 points, while Malaysia landed in fourth place on 152 points.

National juries in the participating countries and the viewing audience awarded the points.

The competition featured motifs inspired by host city Bangkok, with the participants making their way to the stage on tuk-tuks and waving the flag of the countries they represent in a parade.

Will the Eurovision Song Contest Asia become a sensation?

The contest featured some references to the camp European competition. Bulgarian singer Dara performed "Bangaranga," the song which won the Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna in May. 

It's unclear whether Eurovision Song Contest Asia will be as popular as the original competition, which received 131 million viewers this year. Tickets for the Bangkok event were still available just hours before it kicked off.

In 2022, a US spinoff, the American Song Contest, featured acts from all 50 US states. The competition, hosted by rapper Snoop Dogg and American Idol star Kelly Clarkson, only lasted for one season.

entries.title: SpaceX carries out first-ever spaceship capture
entries.summary: The successful recovery of SpaceX's Starship marks a breakthrough in founder Elon Musk’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket system.
entries.content:
November 14, 2026

The successful recovery of SpaceX's Starship marks a breakthrough in founder Elon Musk’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket system.

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned from its longest-yet flight in orbit on Saturday to the tower it was launched from on Friday.

The spaceship descended and smoothly slipped between the mechanical "chopstick arms" above Launch Pad 2 in the US state of Texas. It was the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decadelong effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.

"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted. "Look at her! Baby, she’s back!"

SpaceX's Starship hit key milestone

It was the 15th test flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket system. The Starship spacecraft orbited Earth 14 times for over 22 hours, during which it deployed 26 Starlink satellites.

The successful return marked a ​key milestone in the multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees ​as crucial to SpaceX's satellite business and ambitions to put humans on the Moon and eventually Mars.

NASA welcomed the news. The US space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. 

"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman wrote on X.

SpaceX still investigating booster malfunction

SpaceX also intended to capture the bottom part of the rocket, known as the Super Heavy booster, but the lower stage recovery was aborted, and it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico shortly after launch on Friday.

SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon. The booster's guidance system sensed it was not in the correct position and initiated the self-destruction protocol. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX caught the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights. Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX’s goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.

entries.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
entries.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?
entries.content:
Nigeria

Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation

November 14, 2026

As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

entries.title: South Sudan pushes back elections amid violent flare-ups
entries.summary: South Sudan has been independent from Sudan since 2011, and has not yet held national elections. Since then, the country faces cycles of violence after a civil war led to a tenuous peace deal.
entries.content:
South Sudan

South Sudan pushes back elections amid violent flare-ups

November 14, 2026

South Sudan has been independent from Sudan since 2011, and has not yet held national elections. Since then, the country faces cycles of violence after a civil war led to a tenuous peace deal.

South Sudan on Saturday pushed back its first national elections from December to February next year, as the country faces flare-ups of violence and political strife.   

Why were the elections pushed back?

Presidential and legislative elections are now slated for February 11, 2027. 

"We didn't postpone the elections. We have just adjusted the time to allow other processes to be implemented and that is according to the law," National Elections Commission spokeswoman and Commissioner Josephine Achiro said.

"Article 57 of the National Elections Commission gives us authority to adjust the elections timelines," she added.

Achiro said the postponement of the election date is for voter registration and civic education purposes.

According to the World Bank, the vast majority of South Sudanese lack state-recognized ID, creating challenges for voter registration. Thousands of centers have been established across the country to register voters.

What is the political situation in South Sudan?

South Sudan became independent from Sudan in July 2011 following a referendum. The country has some 12 million people and is one of the impoverished nations on the planet. 

From 2013 to 2018, forces backed by President Silva Kiir, a member of the Dinka ethnic group, fought against troops supported by Vice President Riek Machar, who hails from the Nuer tribe. More than 400,000 people died in that conflict.

A fragile peace agreement was achieved between the two sides in 2018, with a national unity government established in 2020.

Kiir dissolved South Sudan's transitional government in September ahead of elections, and has since ruled by decree in a caretaker administration. He fired Vice President Machar, who had earlier been charged with treason and is under house arrest.

Despite the peace deal, there are also frequent clashes between the Dinka and Nuer groups loyal to Kiir and Machar.

Growing violence

The head of the UN Mission in South Sudan, Anita Kiki Ghebo, said earlier in the week that violence is increasing and added that approximately 10 million people in South Sudan need some form of humanitarian assistance. She also noted that 1.4 million people have entered South Sudan due to an ongoing conflict in Sudan. 

"If left unaddressed, political, security, and humanitarian challenges risk reinforcing one another, further exacerbating tensions adn vulnerabilities across the country," she said.

She has urged renewed dialogue "to focus on establishing clear and credible roadmap for completing the outstanding provisions of the Revitalized Peace Agreement," the formal name for the 2018 peace deal.

entries.title: US: Duffy says 'incompetence' or bad tech to blame for flight haltings
entries.summary: Air carriers in the US canceled some 16,000 flights over the past 24 hours in the biggest such grounding since 9/11. Officials hinted that incompetence or faulty equipment, not malfeasance, is the cause.
entries.content:
United States of America

US: Duffy says 'incompetence' or bad tech to blame for flight haltings

November 14, 2026

Air carriers in the US canceled some 16,000 flights over the past 24 hours in the biggest such grounding since 9/11. Officials hinted that incompetence or faulty equipment, not malfeasance, is the cause.

US Federal Aviation Administration officials and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday said that investigations are ongoing in an attempt to find the cause of the largest mass grounding of flights in the country in over 25 years.

Stranded passengers scrambled to find hotel rooms or buses and trains that could take them to their destinations, others hunkered down in the nation's airports in the first such nationwide grounding since January 2023 and the largest since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks.

International carriers were also forced to cancel flights to the US, and the massive backlog prompted, among other things, the rescheduling of dozens of college and professional sporting events — a staple of many Americans' weekends.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said that a total of 16,000 flights had been delayed on Friday and Saturday, adding that he hoped flight schedules would be back to normal sometime Sunday, saying the "worst is behind us."

Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks to deflect blame

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said no evidence of malfeasance had been found, before pointing his finger at numerous possible culprits, starting with the previous administration, then Congress and eventually settling on possible "contractor incompetence."

Duffy said the issue may have been a faulty router installed when workers from "legacy contractor" L3Harris replaced aged copper wire with new fiberoptic cable or that they had somehow caused a system overload while updating the wires.

During a press conference that was itself plagued with technical problems, Duffy said, "We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning, was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said, adding that either way, "Our contractor didn't meet the moment."

He was also asked why such complicated updates would be undertaken on a Friday afternoon when air travel is at its busiest rather than on a Saturday night, for instance, when far-fewer planes are in the air. He replied by saying the scheduling of such updates will be reevaluated moving forward.

Since the decision was made to update the very old infrastructure currently in use, Congress has approved $12.5 billion (€11.3 billion) to fund the changeover. The Trump administration had been seeking a further $30 billion to complete the job but Duffy on Friday called $50 billion instead, saying, "This is an emergency."

Who will compensate customers?

Despite the pain and frustration endured by customers, there is also a massive financial component to the groundings.

Since the groundings were ordered by the FAA, airlines are not legally responsible for compensating passengers whose flights were cancelled.

On Saturday, Administrator Bedford said the FAA is "working with aviation stakeholders" to make things right, saying, "everyone will either be reaccommodated (sic) on a flight or they'll get a full refund."

Investors are already beginning to calculate potential losses to airlines — which will compound the sting of sky-high fuel prices brought on by the Trump administration's war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz — with shares of American, Delta and United Airlines falling between 1% and 2% late Friday.

Shares in JetBlue as well as contractor L3Harris were down 3%.

entries.title: Fact check: 'Iranian' content farms reach millions
entries.summary: Several social media accounts claiming to represent the Iranian military show signs of being part of so-called content farms. DW Fact Check looks at how they operate and how users can spot them.
entries.content:
Iran

Fact check: 'Iranian' content farms reach millions

November 14, 2026

Several social media accounts claiming to represent the Iranian military show signs of being part of so-called content farms. DW Fact Check looks at how they operate and how users can spot them.

As fears of regional escalation grew after US strikes on Iran, US President Donald Trump claimed the US-Israel war with Iran was "effectively over" on November 9 at a White House briefing. "We're just keeping it the status quo."

Periods of heightened public interest, such as the conflict involving Iran, create fertile ground for so-called content farms. Following Trump's statement, posts on the Iran war surged online again. And a growing network of accounts claiming links to Iran's military has accumulated millions of views.

DW Fact Check examined a number of these accounts and found recurring signs of content farm behavior. Experts who reviewed the accounts DW provided describe them as part of a broader ecosystem of pro-Iran content aggregators that connect across multiple social media platforms. 

Content farms are websites or social media accounts, or a network of either, producing large amounts of cheap content in a short time span. They may be driven by economic incentives, but they can also serve as vehicles for political influence campaigns.  

Content farming and the Iran war

The internet watchdog NewsGuard has found 165 false claims about the Iran warthat collectively have been watched hundreds of millions of times. Only a few of them originated from Iranian state media. 

NewsGuard identified the majority as pushing a pro-Iran agenda, shifting toward AI-generated images, and increasingly claiming that accurate stories from authentic media are AI-generated and false.

An analysis by the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) identified pro-Iran networks of X accounts which revealed signs of coordination, cross-promotion and engagement tactics while spreading misleading and AI-generated war content. It found no links to state-affiliated actors. 

Several accounts identified by DW Fact Check use the Iranian flag as their profile picture and a variation of "Iran Military" in their username. While ownership cannot always be verified, they share recurring characteristics commonly associated with content farms.

A network reaching millions

Content farms use repetitive and formulaic posting formats, as they are cheaper and easier to produce. Their posts frequently start with the word "BREAKING" and imitate the appearance of news updates on the conflict.

One account, called "Iran Military Media," is linked to a Facebook account that Iranian state media have verified as authentic. It has built a substantial audience across multiple social media platforms, with over 290,000 followers on X, 597,000 on Facebook and 17,200 followers on Instagram.

It posts a handful of times a day, often sharing AI-generated or AI-enhanced videos and frequently adopting the "BREAKING" format. Since late 2025, it has published more than 1,600 posts on X, generating over 150 million views and 3.6 million likes.

"The accounts discussed are a central part of this ecosystem as they distribute the pro-Iranian content, state and non-state allied media at relatively low cost and generate millions of views," said Moustafa Ayad, an expert in online influence operations at the ISD.

Iran's 'soft war'

Ayad examined 10 similar "Iran Military"-themed accounts during the same period, and their combined reach is even greater. Together, they accounted for 12,588 posts, 353 million views and 6.6 million likes.

This network is replicated on Facebook in numerous languages. According to Ayad, this strategy is part of what the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei outlined as "soft war."

Ayad said the accounts' reach is amplified when they are paired with other accounts. Only a small share of "Iran Military Media's" 150 million views came from reposted content.

False narratives

A second account, "Iranian Force," has amassed more than 248,000 followers. It typically posts around 10 times a day, though on some days the volume exceeds 30 posts. 

Like "Iran Military Media," it frequently relies on "BREAKING" alerts and AI-generated content. It also includes genuine footage, often framed through a pro-Iran lens. 

X lists the account as being based in Pakistan and its profile history shows six username changes. In a break from the Iran-related content, one post suddenly defends a Pakistani TikToker and includes an appeal in Urdu to the government in Pakistan.

Charlene Lin, an analyst for the internet watchdog NewsGuard, told DW it had flagged this account for multiple false narratives. According to Lin, it is also linked to another account that spreads the same false narratives in coordination.

Unverified claims

A third account, called the "Iran Army," posts a handful of times a day, including AI-generated videos. Its posts regularly reach tens and at times hundreds of thousands of views. 

Like "Iranian Force," it distributes videos from official briefings by the Iranian Armed Forces while also using the "BREAKING" format to drive engagement. One post claiming "the war has officially started" received over 41 million views.

While these accounts differ in reach and post slightly different content, they share many characteristics. The accounts repeatedly share cheaply produced images, at times coordinated between accounts, and make sensational and unverified claims portraying Iran as militarily powerful or politically influential.

Several accounts in this wider ecosystem have faced restrictions. Since March, a number of prominent "Iran Military"-themed accounts have been suspended on X, including "Iran Military Monitor," which had close to 2 million followers before its removal.

A consistent pro-Iran framing

Earlier this year, Iranian state media issued a statement distancing itself from a range of "Iran Military" accounts circulating on social media, stating that only one account was authentic. 

Yet for social media users, distinguishing that account from the others may not be straightforward. The verified account uses the same "Iran Military" branding and a similar profile picture, while also sharing AI-generated content and frequent "BREAKING" updates.

Despite differences in authenticity and affiliation, many of these accounts consistently adopt a pro-Iran framing. They portray Iran as militarily capable, able to retaliate against adversaries and enjoying international support, while rarely highlighting information that contradicts that image.

DW Fact Check found repeated postings of the same content close in time across the accounts and different platforms. The "Iranian Force" and "Iran Military Media" accounts have, for example, posted the same image (here and here), with the same caption on the same day, as have accounts in the wider "Iran Military Media" network.

"The pro-Iranian ecosystem online is large, multi-layered and cuts across almost all of the various popular social media platforms and messaging services," said the ISD's Ayad. "[It's] a key component to the Iranian government's ability to withstand challenges to its rule both from within and outside, while generating sympathy and connections with other online communities."

entries.title: Italy slaps Meta with €805mn fine over access to Android photos
entries.summary: Italian regulators say Meta accessed photos and multimedia content from Italian users via the Facebook application for Android devices. Meta said it would appeal the decision, calling the fine "disproportionate."

entries.title: COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal
entries.summary: The UN climate chief has warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal

November 14, 2026

The UN climate chief has warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.

The United Nations' top climate official urged negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to "avoid tactical delays" that would prevent a deal to stop global warming.

Delegates from more than 200 nations are gathered in the Mediterranean city of Antalya with the core goal of preventing the planet from warming by 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit). 

Downtown, thousands of civil society and environmental activists from around the world protested against the consequences of climate change.

What did the UN climate chief say?

Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), said getting an agreement is "tough but vital work."

"There ​is no collective success without compromise from every party," he added.

"As we head into the second week, ​I urge ‌parties to move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays."

Climate protest draws activists from around the world

Meanwhile, tens of thousands of protesters marched through Antalya on Saturday for climate protection and human rights, according to organizers.

Many were dismayed at the lack of progress and how the climate crisis is taking a back seat.

"The pursuit of profit at all costs continues to set the [global] agenda [and] govern the trajectory of our world, so there is a need to push back," environmental activist Zaki Mamdoo from South Africa told DW.

Luisa Nebauer, the main organizer of Germany's Fridays for Future movement, lamented that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was absent from the conference, along with several other European leaders.

"We won't have a chance to solve any of the crises as long as our planet is destabilizing by the hour," Nebauer told DW. "We must show up!"

Turkish authorities permitted the rally to go ahead, in a country that often bans large public gatherings.

Alongside the march, a parallel "People's Climate Summit" involving hundreds of domestic and international civil society groups takes place in Antalya this weekend.

Climate crisis pushed down agenda

With inflation, wars, deindustrialization and debt being seen as bigger immediate threats, many governments are watering down their commitments to the clean energy transition, along with the billions required to help developing nations to adapt.

The United ⁠States has snubbed the talks ​for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.

Delegates also face pressure from large fossil-fuel-producing nations to avoid setting stricter targets for a faster phaseout of oil and gas.

Climate advocates in Antalya are growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of commitment and delaying tactics preventing an ambitious deal.

COP31 is seeking to unlock finance and investment, reduce the use of so-called super-pollutants and methane and ensure food security.

Turkey seeks electrification deal

Host Turkey is, meanwhile, pushing a plan to expand global electrification. Yet, some environmental groups are disappointed the proposal doesn't push increased electricity use from renewable sources.

A UN report last month warned that, within a few years, the world is set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming.

The figure, set at COP21 in 2015, is the threshold beyond which most scientists believe the world will see increasingly extreme effects of climate change.

A first draft of a deal text is expected to emerge next week, according to Australia's ​COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.
